title: Stable, until the mutants meet
hook: No one gains by switching alone. Can a mutant still take over?

doesNotKnow: that if mutants tie with residents but beat each other, they creep in and then take over

misconception: If no single individual gains by switching, no mutant can ever spread.
objective: The learner can explain that all-A is a Nash equilibrium (B ties A against A) but not an ESS (B scores 3 against B, A only 1), so B's edge, which grows with how often B's meet, lets 1% B creep to 2% by generation 50 and then sweep to 99% by generation 111.

claims.text: With payoff = surviving offspring and no baseline (A vs A 2, A vs B 1, B vs A 2, B vs B 3), everyone playing A is a Nash equilibrium: B earns 2 against A, the same as A, so no one gains by switching alone.
claims.source: Against an all-A population: A earns 2, B earns 2; switching gives no gain. Demo.tsx wA/wB. Our own payoffs.

claims.text: With these payoffs (surviving offspring, no baseline) all-A is not an evolutionarily stable strategy, because B ties A against A and does better against B (3) than A does against B (1).
claims.source: ESS conditions (Maynard Smith & Price 1973): A is an ESS iff E(A,A) > E(B,A), or E(A,A) = E(B,A) and E(A,B) > E(B,B). Here E(A,A) = E(B,A) = 2 and E(A,B) = 1 < E(B,B) = 3. Easley & Kleinberg (2010) ch. 7 (section unconfirmed). Attribution: fact-checker to confirm.

claims.text: In the stage's update rule (surviving offspring, no baseline; share y' = y·W_B / mean W), B rises from 1% to 1.1% by generation 10, 2.0% by 50, 21% by 100 and 99% by 111.
claims.source: Builder's Node run, 2026-10-14 (deterministic, no random seed): 0.0111 at 10, 0.0196 at 50, 0.2104 at 100, first ≥ 0.99 at 111 (0.9963). The no-baseline choice matters: with a baseline of 10 offspring the climb is about six times slower (2.9% at generation 400 in the builder's run), so the stage says 'no baseline'.

claims.text: With B share y, A averages 2 − y and B averages 2 + y, so B's edge is 2y: 0.02 at 1%, 0.42 at 21%; it grows as B's meet each other more often.
claims.source: A: 2(1 − y) + 1·y = 2 − y. B: 2(1 − y) + 3y = 2 + y. Stage readout 'B's edge over A'. Builder's Node run, 2026-10-14.

claims.text: The model is a toy: chosen payoffs, no baseline offspring, random meetings in a very large population; it is not a claim about a real species.
claims.source: Model choice in Demo.tsx, stated on the stage and in the reveal.

recall.question: Mutants tie with residents when they meet residents, but do better than residents when they meet each other. What happens to a few mutants?
options: They creep in slowly, then take over
They die out, because nobody gains by switching alone
They stay at the same small share forever
recall.why: Their edge comes only from meeting each other, which is rare at first. As their share grows the edge grows, so the spread speeds up. A Nash equilibrium is not necessarily evolutionarily stable.
